quote: eight bytes of header with two ports, a length and a checksum
problem: Nothing up to here says what a transport port is. Part III has only shown switch ports (ch8-ethernet) and NAT port numbers (ch9-v6), never what a port is for. So this reader cannot say why 'destination port 53' means DNS, what 'source port 51234' is, or what UDP adds to IP at all, since p1 called it 'just send packets'. The old caption's gloss ('which service to deliver to') was dropped in the redraw, and neither the drawing nor the strip nor the prose puts it back.
fix: one clause: a port is a number that says which program on the machine gets the bytes (53 is the DNS server's; the sender picks its own so the reply can find it)
reason: Checked Parts I to III before ch10: ports appear only as switch ports (ch8) and as NAT table entries (ch9 caption), never as the number that picks the receiving program. Fig 10.1 draws 'destination port 53 · DNS' and the caption names 'two ports' with no gloss, so the reader cannot say what 53 means or why UDP is more than 'just send packets'. Fig 10.1 is a redraw, not kept-original, so the caption can carry the fix.
judge_fix: Caption ch10-udp-p3, first sentence: 'UDP is an envelope around your bytes: eight bytes of header with a length, a checksum and two ports (numbers saying which program on each machine the bytes belong to: 53 is a DNS server's), and nothing else.' Leave the second sentence as is.

quote: TCP's three-message setup (Section 03) would double the time the lookup takes
problem: If you count messages, three setup messages plus a request and a response come to five, not double the two. The reader is never told that the time is counted in round trips, or that the third setup message goes out together with the request. So the setup adds one round trip to a lookup that takes one round trip.
fix: 'adds a full round trip before the question can even go out, doubling a one-round-trip lookup'
reason: Low severity. The claim is true in time (the handshake costs one round trip before the request can leave, so a one-round-trip lookup doubles), but 'three-message setup' next to a two-message lookup does not add up on its face, and 'round trip' is not yet tied to the handshake (Section 03 does that later). One short phrase repairs it.
judge_fix: '...TCP's three-message setup (Section 03) would add a full round trip before the question could even go out, doubling the time the lookup takes, for nothing.'

quote: the congestion-control state, and a few dozen other values
problem: The reader has never met congestion control. p1 has just said every piece of TCP's machinery serves one of four goals, and this item fits none of them, so the reader stops to ask whether it is flow control under another name or a fifth goal. It is never explained in this section; Section 04's title (Flow and congestion control) is the first sign that it is a separate thing.
fix: a short clause such as 'congestion control (slowing down when the network itself is overloaded, Section 04)', and a softer p1 claim, or drop the item from the list
reason: ch10-why-p1 says 'Every piece of machinery TCP carries serves one of those four goals', yet p3 lists congestion-control state and Section 04 presents congestion control as a separate, deeper problem. Factually, the 1974 Cerf and Kahn design had no congestion control; Jacobson and Karels added it in 1988, which Section 04 itself says. So p1's universal claim is false as written, and the TCB list then contradicts it.
judge_fix: p1 last sentence: 'Everything in the 1974 design serves one of those four goals; the one large later addition, congestion control, is the subject of Section 04.' p3: 'the congestion-control state (Section 04), and a few dozen other values.'

quote: acknowledges the client's plus one
problem: The reader has not yet been told that an acknowledgement names the next byte the receiver expects; the book first says so in Fig 10.4 in ch10-aimd. So 'plus one', and the strip's 'SYN counts as one byte', still leave them expecting ack 4170, since 4170 is the number they received.
fix: one clause in the caption or the 'Plus one' strip: an ACK names the next byte it expects, and SYN used up 4170, so the ACK says 4171
reason: The book never says an acknowledgement names the next byte expected until Fig 10.4 (ch10-aimd), after the handshake. The 'Plus one' strip says SYN counts as a byte but leaves the reader expecting ack 4170, the number they received. A single clause closes it.
judge_fix: Fig 10.2 strip, 'Plus one': 'An acknowledgement names the next byte expected, and SYN counts as one byte of sequence space, so the acknowledgements are 4171 and 9013.'

quote: Most connections take one well-trodden path
problem: Fig 10.2 has just shown the server going LISTEN → SYN_RCVD → ESTABLISHED in an ordinary handshake. The prose then gives a single path through SYN_SENT and says the off-path states handle simultaneous opens, closes and lost FINs, which contradicts that figure. The reader cannot tell whether SYN_RCVD is normal or a failure state until the Fig 10.3 caption says which side is which.
fix: say this is the path of the side that opens and closes first; add the server's path (LISTEN, SYN_RCVD, ESTABLISHED, CLOSE_WAIT, LAST_ACK); keep 'off-path' for CLOSING and the rare moves
reason: p3 gives the client path as 'the' well-trodden path and then calls the remaining states 'off-path' for simultaneous opens, closes and lost FINs. SYN_RCVD, CLOSE_WAIT and LAST_ACK are the server's ordinary path, shown in Fig 10.3 and in Fig 10.2 (LISTEN, SYN_RCVD, ESTABLISHED), so the text contradicts the figures until the Fig 10.3 caption sorts it out. The count works: 6 client states + LISTEN, SYN_RCVD, CLOSE_WAIT, LAST_ACK + CLOSING = 11.
judge_fix: Replace the two sentences after 'by fixed rules: a state machine covering setup, data transfer and teardown.' with: 'Most connections take one of two well-trodden paths. The side that connects and closes first goes CLOSED → SYN_SENT → ESTABLISHED → FIN_WAIT_1 → FIN_WAIT_2 → TIME_WAIT → CLOSED; the other goes CLOSED → LISTEN → SYN_RCVD → ESTABLISHED → CLOSE_WAIT → LAST_ACK → CLOSED. The one remaining state, CLOSING, and the side routes exist to handle simultaneous opens, simultaneous closes, lost FINs (the segment that says I have nothing more to send), and the dozen other partial-failure modes the protocol was designed to survive.'

quote: begins cautiously, with a tiny congestion window (cwnd) of one segment
problem: The section's central variable is used as if already known. The prose never says that the congestion window is a second limit on bytes in flight, that the sender keeps it for itself (nobody advertises it), or that the sender sends no more than the smaller of this window and the receive window. Only Fig 10.4's closed strip says so.
fix: name it at first use: the sender's own cap on bytes in flight, its guess at what the network can take; the smaller of the two windows wins
reason: p6 uses cwnd as the central variable and never says it is the sender's own cap, nor how it relates to the receive window just defined in p2. That is stated only in the closed Fig 10.4 strip ('The sender obeys the smaller'), which the reader may never open. The prose should carry the relation at first use.
judge_fix: p6: 'Slow start begins cautiously, with a tiny congestion window (cwnd) of one segment: the sender's own cap on bytes in flight, its guess at what the network can carry. The sender obeys the smaller of this and the receive window, and cwnd _doubles_ on every successful round trip: ...' (rest unchanged).

quote: at a high enough SYN rate the table fills and legitimate clients cannot connect
problem: ch10-why-p3 told the reader that a Linux server holds a million TCBs, and the caption's own numbers (a few thousand SYNs a second, each held about 30 s) come to roughly 100,000 entries, so the reader cannot see why the table fills. Nothing says this table is the 'SYN backlog' that Fig 10.11 later names.
fix: one clause: half-open connections wait in a separate, much smaller queue, the SYN backlog
reason: ch10-why-p3 says a Linux server holds a million TCBs, and p2 then says the table fills at a few thousand SYNs a second (about 100,000 slots at ~30 s). The reader cannot reconcile the two. Half-open connections actually wait in a small, separate queue, the SYN backlog, which Fig 10.11 (kept-original) names without introduction. One clause in p2 fixes both. The Fig 10.10 and 10.11 captions stay untouched.
judge_fix: p2: 'Each half-open connection holds a slot in the SYN backlog, a short queue kept apart from established connections, for tens of seconds (the SYN_RCVD timeout); at a high enough SYN rate the backlog fills and legitimate clients cannot connect.'

quote: a keyed hash of the (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port, time bucket)
problem: No earlier section uses the word 'hash', so the reader cannot say what the server computes or why recomputing it later gives the same number. The closest earlier idea is ch3-defenses-p9's pointer-authentication code, 'computed from it and a key'. Never explained in this section.
fix: a plain gloss: a fixed-size scrambled number computed from those values plus a server secret; same inputs, same number
reason: I grepped Parts I to III: 'hash' is not explained before this point (SHA-256 hashing comes in Ch12, later), and the cookie mechanism rests on 'recompute the hash and compare'. A one-line gloss at first use is cheap and needed. Merge with the fix for #10 and #11 in the same paragraph.
judge_fix: See the combined p4 rewrite in #10.

quote: earns a reconstructed connection and a TCB
problem: A TCB holds 'a few dozen' values (ch10-why-p3) and the cookie is a 32-bit hash, so the reader cannot see how it 'encodes the necessary state' or what the server rebuilds the TCB from. Nothing says the ACK itself brings back the addresses, ports and both sequence numbers.
fix: one sentence: the ACK repeats addresses, ports and sequence numbers; the cookie only proves they answer a real SYN-ACK
reason: p4 says the server 'encodes the necessary state' into a 32-bit keyed hash, which cannot hold addresses, ports and sequence numbers. In reality the returning ACK carries those, and the cookie only proves they answer a real SYN-ACK (plus a few bits of MSS). The Fig 10.11 text (kept-original, 'all state derived from the cookie') is loose, but the prose can be made exact without touching it.
judge_fix: Replace p4 from 'Instead, it encodes' with: 'Instead, it hides what it needs in the Initial Sequence Number (ISN) it returns in the SYN-ACK: a keyed hash (a fixed-size scramble of the values with the server's secret key: the same inputs give the same number) of the source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port and a time bucket, with a few bits for the MSS (the largest segment the client said it accepts, the one setting the server would otherwise have to remember). The whole fits in 32 bits and is hard to forge without the key. The third ACK repeats the addresses, ports and sequence numbers and carries the cookie back (its acknowledgement number is the cookie plus one); the server recomputes the hash from them, and a match proves the ACK answers a SYN-ACK it really sent. Only then does it rebuild the connection and allocate a TCB. Legitimate clients pass; the flood's spoofed connections never send an ACK at all.'

quote: a few bits encoding the MSS hint the server would normally have remembered
problem: MSS (also drawn in Fig 10.11 as 'MSS hint') has never been expanded or explained, so the reader cannot say what setting the cookie has to carry or why the server would normally have remembered it. This caption is kept original, so the fix belongs in prose.
fix: in p4's prose: MSS, the largest segment the client will accept, the one setting squeezed into a few cookie bits
reason: MSS is never expanded or explained in Parts I to III (only appears in the kept-original Fig 10.11 and its caption). The caption itself cannot be changed, so the prose must define it; the combined p4 rewrite under #10 does so.
judge_fix: Covered in the #10 rewrite: 'a few bits for the MSS (the largest segment the client said it accepts...)'. If the owner wants it shorter: 'plus a few bits for the MSS, the largest segment size the client accepts'.

quote: injects a TCP RST (reset) segment with a sequence number in the receiver's window
problem: The reader is never told that a receiver ignores segments numbered outside its window, or that an attacker on the path can read the current numbers off the passing traffic. Without that, they cannot say why this attack 'turns on sequence numbers' or how it differs from hijacking, which has to predict the numbers.
fix: a clause: out-of-window segments are ignored, and an on-path attacker reads the live numbers off the traffic
reason: p6 says the RST must carry a sequence number 'in the receiver's window' but never says out-of-window segments are ignored, nor that an on-path attacker can read the live numbers. Without both, the reader cannot see why this attack 'turns on sequence numbers' or how it differs from hijacking (which must predict them). The clause is short and true.
judge_fix: '*RST injection*: an attacker on the path, who can read the live sequence numbers off the traffic, injects a TCP RST (reset) segment numbered inside the receiver's window (anything outside it is ignored), causing the receiver to tear down the connection.'

quote: SYN-flooded a trusted host on Shimomura's network to take it out of the conversation
problem: The reader cannot say why the trusted host had to be silenced. p2 said a SYN-ACK sent to an uninvolved host simply goes unanswered, and nothing says that the real host, getting a SYN-ACK it never asked for, would answer with a RST and kill the forged connection.
fix: a clause: otherwise it would answer the unexpected SYN-ACK with a RST, tearing the forged connection down
reason: Historically correct: Mitnick silenced the trusted host so it would not answer the workstation's SYN-ACK with a RST that kills the forged connection. The text says only 'take it out of the conversation', and p2 told the reader that an uninvolved host's SYN-ACK 'goes nowhere', so the reader cannot see why silencing was needed.
judge_fix: 'Mitnick SYN-flooded a trusted host on Shimomura's network so that it could not answer with a RST to the SYN-ACK it had never asked for (which would have torn the forged connection down), then opened a TCP connection...'

quote: the network can never authenticate who you are, only what you say
problem: Taken literally, it says the network does authenticate what you say, but the section has just shown that forged addresses and forged segments are accepted at face value. The reader re-reads to work out what the slogan means.
fix: plain words: the network checks nothing; it carries whatever address and bytes a sender writes
reason: Low severity. Read literally, the line implies the network does authenticate 'what you say', yet the section has just shown it accepts forged addresses and forged segments at face value. The intended point (the network verifies nothing, so applications must) is lost to the flourish. A short plain rewrite keeps the lesson and the TLS link.
judge_fix: 'The deeper lesson is that the network checks nothing about who is sending: it carries whatever address and bytes a sender writes, so applications must authenticate cryptographically on top.'

quote: random ISNs (state in the unguessable), TLS (state cryptographically authenticated)
problem: The strip presents all three defences as 'making the protocol stateless under attack', but random ISNs and TLS keep their state. The reader cannot see how they make anything stateless, and the closing 'pushes state into harder places' says something different.
fix: say SYN cookies remove state, while random ISNs and TLS make the state that remains unguessable or unforgeable
reason: The strip says all three defences make the protocol 'stateless under attack', but only SYN cookies remove state; random ISNs and TLS leave state in place and protect it. The parenthetical glosses ('state in the unguessable') are opaque and the closing sentence ('pushes state into harder places') says something different from the sentence before it.
judge_fix: 'The defences are nearly all about moving or protecting that state: SYN cookies put it in the wire, random ISNs make the state that remains unguessable, TLS makes it cryptographically authenticated.' Keep the closing sentence as is.

quote: The off-path states exist to handle simultaneous opens, simultaneous closes, lost FINs
problem: The path the paragraph gives is only the client's: it opens the connection and closes first. The states left off it are LISTEN, SYN_RCVD, CLOSE_WAIT, LAST_ACK and CLOSING. The first four are the normal path of every server that answers a connection and closes second, and Fig 10.3 and its caption draw them that way. Only CLOSING is kept for a simultaneous close. No state exists for lost FINs: retransmission timers handle them (RFC 793, Fig. 6). As written, a reader learns that the server's ordinary states are failure handlers.
fix: Replace the last two sentences with: "A client usually walks CLOSED → SYN_SENT → ESTABLISHED → FIN_WAIT_1 → FIN_WAIT_2 → TIME_WAIT → CLOSED; the server it talks to walks LISTEN → SYN_RCVD → ESTABLISHED → CLOSE_WAIT → LAST_ACK → CLOSED. The remaining rules handle simultaneous opens and closes, lost FINs (the segment that says I have nothing more to send) and the other partial failures the protocol was designed to survive."
reason: Checked against the section: the listed path is the client's. LISTEN, SYN_RCVD, CLOSE_WAIT and LAST_ACK are the server's ordinary states, and the Fig 10.3 caption and strip draw them that way. CLOSING is the only state kept for a simultaneous close. No state exists for lost FINs; timers handle those. As written, a reader learns the server's normal states are failure handlers.
judge_fix: Replace the last two sentences of ch10-handshake-p3 with: "A client usually walks CLOSED → SYN_SENT → ESTABLISHED → FIN_WAIT_1 → FIN_WAIT_2 → TIME_WAIT → CLOSED; the server it talks to walks LISTEN → SYN_RCVD → ESTABLISHED → CLOSE_WAIT → LAST_ACK → CLOSED. Each side closes by sending a FIN (the segment that says I have nothing more to send). The remaining rules handle simultaneous opens and closes and the other partial failures the protocol was designed to survive." The "Most connections take one well-trodden path" sentence is dropped, since the two-path wording replaces it. The FIN gloss stays, so the first-use definition is kept.

quote: It is what the great majority of internet TCP traffic runs.
problem: Measurement says otherwise. The 2019 census (Mishra et al., "The Great Internet TCP Congestion Control Census", Proc. ACM Meas. Anal. Comput. Syst. 3(3), 2019) found CUBIC on about 36% of the Alexa top 20,000 sites. BBR was on 22% of sites, but its estimated share of traffic volume was "larger than 40%". So CUBIC runs on the most servers, not on the great majority of traffic.
fix: "It is the most common TCP algorithm on web servers (about a third of the top 20,000 sites in a 2019 census), though BBR, next, already carried an estimated two-fifths of the traffic."
reason: Mishra et al. (2019 census) put CUBIC on the most sites but BBR on an estimated 40%+ of downstream traffic volume, so "great majority of internet TCP traffic" is unsupported. No §4g row backs it. The paragraph after it introduces BBR, so the fix should not undercut that.
judge_fix: Replace the last sentence of ch10-modern-p2 with: "It is the algorithm most web servers run." Add no percentage. The next paragraphs introduce BBR, and a 2019 share figure would date quickly.

quote: BBR can be two to ten times faster than CUBIC
problem: No source gives this range. Google's own figures (Google Cloud blog, July 2017) are: 2,700 times CUBIC's throughput on a 10 Gbit/s, 100 ms path with 1% loss, a microbenchmark; 4% more throughput across YouTube; and, behind an oversized queue, 25 times less queueing delay (43 ms against 1,090 ms) with no throughput gain. Behind home routers with oversized queues BBR's win is lower delay, not speed, because CUBIC fills those links too.
fix: "On long paths with random loss BBR can move many times more data than CUBIC; behind home routers with oversized queues its gain is delay, not speed, keeping round trips short where CUBIC fills the queue. Across YouTube it raised throughput by 4 percent and cut round-trip time by a third." (source: cloud.google.com/blog/products/networking/tcp-bbr-congestion-control-comes-to-gcp-your-internet-just-got-faster)
reason: Fetched Google's July 2017 BBR post. The figures there are: 2,700x CUBIC's throughput on a 10 Gbit/s, 100 ms path with 1% loss (a synthetic microbenchmark, which the post says is not the typical magnitude); 4% more throughput across YouTube; round-trip time down 33%; and, behind a 1000-packet buffer, queueing delay 25x lower (43 ms against 1,090 ms). "Two to ten times" appears in none of it, and on oversized-queue home routers the gain is delay, not speed. This also mismatches the book's own Fig 10.8, which shows the same delivery rate past the knee.
judge_fix: Replace "On lossy Wi-Fi, transcontinental links and home routers with oversized queues, BBR can be two to ten times faster than CUBIC." with: "On long paths with random loss BBR can move many times more data than CUBIC; behind home routers with oversized queues its gain is delay, not speed, because it keeps the queue short where CUBIC fills it. Across YouTube it raised throughput by 4 percent and cut round-trip time by a third." Source: cloud.google.com/blog/products/networking/tcp-bbr-congestion-control-comes-to-gcp-your-internet-just-got-faster

quote: By 2024 it carried well over a quarter of web requests, and the share is growing.
problem: Cloudflare Radar's Year in Review puts HTTP/3, and so QUIC, at 20% of requests in 2023, 20.5% in 2024 and about 21% in 2025: one request in five, not well over a quarter, and almost flat. The paragraph also disagrees with Ch11's "roughly a third of web traffic by volume" (a different measure; Ch11's checker should confirm it).
fix: "By 2024 about one web request in five used it (20.5 percent of those Cloudflare saw), and the share is creeping up." (source: blog.cloudflare.com/radar-2024-year-in-review)
reason: Fetched Cloudflare's Radar 2024 Year in Review: "20.5% of requests in 2024 were made using HTTP/3", and usage was "up slightly from 2023". Well over a quarter is wrong for 2024. Ch11 line 4463 says "roughly a third of web traffic by volume", a different measure and also unsourced. Flag that line for the Ch11 checker; it is not in this chapter.
judge_fix: Replace the last sentence of ch10-modern-p6 with: "By 2024 about one web request in five used it (20.5 percent of those Cloudflare saw), and the share is creeping up." Source: blog.cloudflare.com/radar-2024-year-in-review

quote: when an attacker can predict the sequence numbers of an existing connection, they can inject data into it
problem: The definition does not fit the story it introduces. Morris's 1985 report (Bell Labs CSTR 117) described opening a new connection in a trusted host's name by guessing the server's next ISN. Mitnick's attack in p7 does the same: a new spoofed connection, not injection into an open one. In Shimomura's own account (Jan 1995), the takeover of an existing session came later and used a kernel STREAMS module on a machine already broken into, not sequence prediction.
fix: "*TCP hijacking*: an attacker who can predict the sequence numbers a host will use can forge segments in another machine's name, opening a connection that seems to come from a trusted host or injecting data into one already open." (keep the key-term span on "TCP hijacking")
reason: Verified in the text. The key-term definition says injecting data into an existing connection. The Morris 1985 report and the Christmas 1994 attack as p7 tells it are blind spoofing of a new connection by predicting the ISN. The definition does not fit its own example.
judge_fix: In ch10-attacks-p6, replace "when an attacker can predict the sequence numbers of an existing connection, they can inject data into it pretending to be one of the endpoints" with: "an attacker who can predict the sequence numbers a host will use can forge segments in another machine's name: opening a connection that seems to come from a trusted host, or injecting data into one already open." Keep the key-term span on "TCP hijacking".

quote: The random ISN requirement (Bellovin's RFC 1948)
problem: RFC 1948 (May 1996) is Informational ("does not specify an Internet standard"), so it is not a requirement. It says outright that "simple randomization ... will not work well". What it proposed was the cryptographic scheme the next sentence credits to 2012: ISN = clock + F(four-tuple), where F is a keyed cryptographic hash such as MD5. RFC 6528 (2012) made that same scheme the standard. The paragraph splits one fix into a random step and a later cryptographic step. The ledger's timing (about a year, stacks took the decade) stays.
fix: "Bellovin's RFC 1948, about a year after Mitnick's arrest, proposed the cure: start each connection's sequence numbers at a clock plus a keyed cryptographic hash of its addresses and ports, so no connection's numbers reveal another's. Stacks took the rest of the decade to adopt it, and RFC 6528 made it the standard in 2012." Keep "random ISN" (or say "unpredictable ISNs") wherever the glossary term needs it.
reason: Fetched RFC 1948. It is Informational, so "requirement" overstates it. It says "simple randomization ... will not work well". It already proposes ISN = M + F(four-tuple, secret) with F a cryptographic hash (MD5 suggested). RFC 6528 (2012) moved that scheme to the standards track. So "random ISN" for 1996 followed by "cryptographically" for 2012 splits one fix in two. The ledger timing (about a year, then the rest of the decade) holds.
judge_fix: Replace the first two sentences of ch10-attacks-p8 with: "The fix, unpredictable ISNs, came from Bellovin's RFC 1948 about a year after Mitnick's arrest: start each connection at a clock plus a keyed hash of its addresses and ports, so one connection's numbers reveal nothing about the next. The stacks took the rest of the decade to adopt it, and RFC 6528 made it the standard in 2012." Keep the rest of the paragraph, dropping "so that sequence numbers cannot be predicted" if it now repeats. Also change "random ISNs" to "unpredictable ISNs" in ch10-attacks-p9, which is not owner text, to avoid a mismatch.

quote: Every piece of machinery TCP carries serves one of those four goals.
problem: Congestion control serves none of the four 1974 goals. Section 04 says flow control "does nothing to prevent the sender from outrunning the network" and dates congestion control to 1988, yet p3 of this section lists congestion-control state in the TCB. A careful reader hits the contradiction two sections later.
fix: "Almost every piece of machinery TCP carries serves one of those four goals; the big exception, congestion control, came fourteen years later (Section 04)."
reason: ch10-why-p1 says every piece of machinery serves one of the four 1974 goals. ch10-why-p3 lists congestion-control state in the TCB. Section 04 says flow control does not stop the sender outrunning the network, and congestion control dates to 1988. UNDER.md also notes the 1974 design had no congestion control. A careful reader hits the contradiction two sections later.
judge_fix: Replace the last sentence of ch10-why-p1 with: "Almost every piece of machinery TCP carries serves one of those four goals; the exception, congestion control, came fourteen years later (Section 04)."

quote: DNS, every video call, every game, every connection over QUIC
problem: "Every game" is false: many games run over TCP (World of Warcraft, most turn-based and mobile games over HTTP or WebSockets). Video calls fall back to TCP when UDP is blocked.
fix: "(DNS, most video calls and fast-paced games, every connection over QUIC, the newer transport of Section 05)"
reason: "Every game" and "every video call" are false. Many games run over TCP, and calls fall back to TCP when UDP is blocked. Low severity, but an easy repair of a plain overclaim.
judge_fix: In ch10-udp-p1, replace "(DNS, every video call, every game, every connection over QUIC, the newer transport of Section 05)" with "(DNS, most video calls, most fast-paced games, every connection over QUIC, the newer transport of Section 05)".

quote: collapsed from its design capacity of 32 kilobits per second
problem: Jacobson and Karels say only that throughput "dropped from 32 Kbps to 40 bps". 32 kbit/s was the link's normal throughput, not a design capacity: the ARPANET IMP lines ran at 56 kbit/s.
fix: "collapsed from its usual 32 kilobits per second to roughly 40 bits per second"
reason: Jacobson and Karels write only that throughput "dropped from 32 Kbps to 40 bps". Nothing in the source calls 32 kbit/s a design capacity, and the ARPANET lines of the time ran faster. The invented claim should go; 32000/40 = 800 still holds.
judge_fix: In ch10-aimd-p5, replace "from its design capacity of 32 kilobits per second" with "from its usual 32 kilobits per second".

quote: some of it through cellular networks Shimomura himself had earlier helped secure
problem: No source found says Shimomura helped secure the cellular networks Mitnick used. His cellular work was research into phones' weak privacy (1992 congressional testimony). The final trace was a cellular modem in Raleigh, found with Sprint technicians and direction-finding gear.
fix: "(the last leg through a cellular modem, which he and Sprint technicians tracked by radio)", or drop the parenthesis.
reason: No source says Shimomura helped secure the cellular networks Mitnick used. His work was research into cellular phones' privacy weaknesses, and the final trace was a cellular modem in Raleigh found with Sprint technicians and direction-finding gear. The parenthesis is unsupported, and the sentence reads fine without it.
judge_fix: In ch10-attacks-p7, delete " (some of it through cellular networks Shimomura himself had earlier helped secure)". Alternative: "(the last leg a cellular modem, which he and Sprint technicians tracked by radio)".

quote: opened a TCP connection to Shimomura's main workstation
problem: Shimomura's technical account names the spoofed connection's target "x-terminal": "a diskless SPARCstation running Solaris 1" that he used as an X terminal. It was not his main workstation.
fix: "opened a TCP connection to a diskless workstation Shimomura used as an X terminal" (source: Shimomura's Jan 1995 post, mirrored at pld.cs.luc.edu/courses/447/sum08/class7/shimomura.text)
reason: Shimomura's own January 1995 account names the spoofed connection's target "x-terminal", a diskless SPARCstation he used as an X terminal, not his main workstation. This agrees with the book's other detail that a trusted server was flooded to silence it. The wording should not call it the main workstation.
judge_fix: In ch10-attacks-p7, replace "to Shimomura's main workstation" with "to one of Shimomura's workstations". This avoids the jargon "X terminal" and is accurate.

quote: the reason every modern OS ships with SYN cookie support
problem: Windows' documented SYN-flood defence is SynAttackProtect: fewer SYN-ACK retransmissions and half-open handshakes held in a hash table. Microsoft documents no SYN cookies. Linux and FreeBSD do ship them. Also, "the reason cloud DDoS protection ... exists" overclaims: those services absorb many kinds of flood.
fix: Owner text, so report only. A true version would say "the reason Linux and the BSDs ship SYN cookies, and one of the floods cloud DDoS protection (Cloudflare, AWS Shield) absorbs".
reason: The sentence is in the Fig 10.10 caption (ch10-attacks-p3), a kept-original figure. "Every modern OS ships with SYN cookie support" is wrong for Windows, whose documented defence is SynAttackProtect; Linux and the BSDs do ship cookies. "The reason cloud DDoS protection exists" also overclaims. Factual error in owner text, so report only. Severity L.
judge_fix: If the owner wants it: "the reason Linux and the BSDs ship SYN cookies, and one of the floods that cloud DDoS protection (Cloudflare, AWS Shield) absorbs."

problem: ch10-udp-p1: 'every game' overstates the case. Many online games run over TCP (World of Warcraft is the well-known example, and so are many turn-based and mobile games). 'Every video call' overstates it too: WebRTC calls fall back to TCP/TLS relays when UDP is blocked. 'Most real-time games and video calls' would be accurate.
reason: Duplicate of finding 9; same overclaim in ch10-udp-p1.
judge_fix: Apply the fix for n=9: "most video calls, most fast-paced games".

problem: ch10-why-p1 vs p3: 'Every piece of machinery TCP carries serves one of those four goals' clashes with the TCB's 'congestion-control state'. Congestion control (Jacobson, 1988) protects the network, not the receiver. It was not among the 1974 goals, and Section 04 treats it as separate from flow control.
reason: Duplicate of finding 8; same contradiction between ch10-why-p1 and p3.
judge_fix: Apply the fix for n=8.

problem: ch10-handshake-p3: 'The off-path states exist to handle simultaneous opens, simultaneous closes, lost FINs' is not accurate. Five states are off the listed path: LISTEN, SYN_RCVD, CLOSE_WAIT, LAST_ACK and CLOSING. The first four are the passive (server) side's ordinary path, as Fig 10.3 itself shows. Only CLOSING is used just for simultaneous close, and a simultaneous open reuses SYN_RCVD. A lost FIN is handled by resending it on a timer, plus TIME_WAIT (which is on the path) answering a resent FIN, not by an off-path state.
reason: Duplicate of finding 1; same fix.
judge_fix: Apply the fix for n=1.

problem: ch10-handshake-p3: 'Most connections take one well-trodden path' describes one end only. Each connection has two ends, each with its own path. Also, the side that closes first is not always the client (HTTP servers often close first), though the Fig 10.3 caption frames this correctly as the figure's own scenario.
reason: Covered by finding 1: "Most connections take one well-trodden path" describes the client's end only. The fix for n=1 replaces it with a client path and a server path, which also removes the false suggestion that the client always closes first. The Fig 10.3 caption frames it as the figure's own scenario, so nothing more is needed there.
judge_fix: Apply the fix for n=1.

problem: ch10-aimd-p5: Jacobson and Karels (1988) say the throughput 'dropped from 32 Kbps to 40 bps'. They do not call 32 kbps the path's 'design capacity', and the IMP trunks of the time ran at 56 kbps. 'Its normal throughput of 32 kilobits per second' would match the source. Low severity, and unverified beyond the paper's wording.
reason: Duplicate of finding 11.
judge_fix: Apply the fix for n=11: "from its usual 32 kilobits per second".

problem: ch10-modern-p2 "It is what the great majority of internet TCP traffic runs": Mishra et al.'s TCP congestion-control census (ACM SIGMETRICS 2019, Gordon tool; IETF 2020 slides) estimated BBR variants already carried more than 40% of downstream internet traffic in 2019, while only about 22% of the top 20,000 sites used it. CUBIC is the most common default by host count, but "great majority of traffic" looks overstated. No §4g row sources it. Possible safer wording: "what most internet hosts run" or "the most widely deployed".
reason: Duplicate of finding 2.
judge_fix: Apply the fix for n=2: "It is the algorithm most web servers run."

problem: ch10-modern-p4 "BBR can be two to ten times faster than CUBIC": no §4g row sources the range. Cardwell et al. (ACM Queue 2016) report 2 to 25 times higher throughput on Google's B4 WAN and large gains under random loss. For "home routers with oversized queues" the gain is shorter queueing delay, not a higher rate, and the book's own Fig 10.8 shows loss-based TCP at the same 1 Gbit/s delivery rate past the knee. An attentive reader comparing the two may notice the mismatch. Pin the source, or say what "faster" means there (less waiting).
reason: Duplicate of finding 3. The "two to ten times" range is unsourced, and the book's own Fig 10.8 shows the same delivery rate past the knee.
judge_fix: Apply the fix for n=3.

problem: ch10-modern-p6 "By 2024 it carried well over a quarter of web requests": no §4g row. Cloudflare's own May 2022 to May 2023 analysis put HTTP/3 at about 28% of requests (blog.cloudflare.com/http3-usage-one-year-on). A third-party summary of Cloudflare Radar's 2024 Year in Review gives about 20.5% (I did not confirm this on Cloudflare's own page). W3Techs' roughly 30% counts websites, not requests. On the 2024 figure, "well over a quarter" looks too high. Pin the source and date (for example, "by 2023, more than a quarter of requests Cloudflare sees"), or soften to "about a fifth to a quarter".
reason: Duplicate of finding 4. I verified the Cloudflare Radar 2024 figure myself: 20.5% of requests. The 28% figure is a different, earlier period.
judge_fix: Apply the fix for n=4.

problem: p6–p7: 'TCP hijacking' is defined as injecting data into an existing connection. But Morris's 1985 Bell Labs report and the Christmas 1994 attack as p7 tells it were blind spoofing of a new connection by predicting the server's ISN. In Shimomura's own 25 Jan 1995 account, taking over an existing connection was a later, separate step (a loadable kernel STREAMS module), not the one described. The label does not match the example.
reason: Duplicate of finding 5.
judge_fix: Apply the fix for n=5.

problem: p7: 'cellular networks Shimomura himself had earlier helped secure' is weakly supported. His documented work was cellular-phone security research (Mitnick stole his OKI phone software), and he found Mitnick by cellular direction-finding with Sprint engineers in Raleigh. I found no source saying he had helped secure the networks Mitnick used.
reason: Duplicate of finding 12.
judge_fix: Apply the fix for n=12: delete the parenthesis.

problem: p8: RFC 1948 (1996) was Informational, so 'requirement' overstates it, and it already proposed a keyed-hash (MD5) ISN. 'Modern stacks generate ISNs cryptographically (RFC 6528, 2012)' implies the cryptographic step came only in 2012, when RFC 6528 mainly moved the same scheme onto the standards track.
reason: Duplicate of finding 6. Confirmed against the RFC 1948 text: Informational status, and the keyed-hash (MD5) scheme is already in it.
judge_fix: Apply the fix for n=6.

quote: The off-path states exist to handle simultaneous opens, simultaneous closes, lost FINs
problem: The 'well-trodden path' the paragraph gives is only the client's end. Fig 10.3, directly below, shows every server taking LISTEN → SYN_RCVD → ESTABLISHED → CLOSE_WAIT → LAST_ACK → CLOSED on an ordinary connection. So four of the 'off-path' states are the normal server path, not failure handling, and the prose and the figure contradict each other. This overlaps the open owner call on Fig 10.3 (option a, which would add how a connection closes).
fix: Replace from 'Most connections take one well-trodden path' to the end of the paragraph with: 'A client's end usually runs CLOSED → SYN_SENT → ESTABLISHED → FIN_WAIT_1 → FIN_WAIT_2 → TIME_WAIT → CLOSED; a server's runs CLOSED → LISTEN → SYN_RCVD → ESTABLISHED → CLOSE_WAIT → LAST_ACK → CLOSED. The remaining state, CLOSING, and the extra moves handle simultaneous opens and closes, lost FINs (the segment that says I have nothing more to send) and the other partial failures the protocol was designed to survive.' This also settles owner call Fig 10.3 (a).
reason: Checked against Fig 10.3 and its desc: LISTEN, SYN_RCVD, CLOSE_WAIT and LAST_ACK are the ordinary server path, and only CLOSING is truly off-path. The paragraph's 'off-path states exist to handle simultaneous opens...' is false for four of the eleven states, and it is the root of the Fig 10.3 owner call.
judge_fix: Replace from 'Most connections take one well-trodden path' to the end with: 'A side that has nothing more to send says so with a FIN segment. When the client opens the connection and closes first, its end runs CLOSED → SYN_SENT → ESTABLISHED → FIN_WAIT_1 → FIN_WAIT_2 → TIME_WAIT → CLOSED and the server's runs CLOSED → LISTEN → SYN_RCVD → ESTABLISHED → CLOSE_WAIT → LAST_ACK → CLOSED. The eleventh state, CLOSING, and the extra moves between the others handle simultaneous opens and closes, lost FINs and the other partial failures the protocol was designed to survive.' This also covers owner call 10.3 option (a) in substance.

quote: Every piece of machinery TCP carries serves one of those four goals.
problem: This is untrue of today's TCP, and the chapter itself shows it. Congestion control (Section 04) serves none of the four goals: flow control protects only the receiver (ch10-aimd-p4), and ch10-why-p3 lists 'the congestion-control state' in every TCB. The section title ('still in force') makes the same claim.
fix: 'Every piece of machinery TCP carried in 1974 served one of those four goals; a fifth, congestion control, was added in 1988 (Section 04).'
reason: Congestion control serves none of the four goals; ch10-aimd-p4 says so, and the TCP glossary entry says it 'came later'. The sentence is false for today's TCP.
judge_fix: 'Every piece of machinery in the 1974 design served one of those four goals; a fifth job, congestion control, was added in 1988 (Section 04).'

quote: UDP carries an enormous fraction of modern internet traffic (DNS, every video call, every game
problem: DNS is the chapter's main UDP example (p1, p2, Fig 10.1's '53 · DNS' and 'payload: the DNS query', the strip), yet no earlier chapter teaches it. Ch8 and Ch9 only name it in a layer list. The only gloss in this chapter is in the seam at its very end ('DNS for finding servers by name'). The baseline reader cannot see why a DNS lookup is one small question and one small answer.
fix: At first use: '(DNS, the lookup that turns a name like example.com into an address; every video call, every game, ...)'. Alternatively, in p2: 'A DNS lookup (asking which address a name like example.com stands for, Chapter 11) is a single small request...'
reason: DNS is never taught before Ch11 (Ch8 only names it in a layer list), yet it is the chapter's main UDP example and drives Fig 10.1. One gloss in p2, which the reader meets before the figure, is enough.
judge_fix: In ch10-udp-p2: 'A DNS lookup (the question "which address is example.com?", Chapter 11) is a single small request and a single small response; ...'. Leave p1 as is.

quote: eight bytes of header with two ports, a length and a checksum, and nothing else
problem: A port in the networking sense (a number that names the program at each end) is never taught. The book's only earlier 'port' is a socket on a switch (ch8-ethernet). Fig 10.1 ('source port 51234', 'destination port 53') and ch10-attacks-p4 ('source IP, source port, ...') rely on it. Without it the reader misses the one thing UDP adds to IP: delivery to the right program.
fix: In ch10-udp-p1: 'an eight-byte header on top of IP, mostly two port numbers that name the program at each end (53 means a DNS server).'
reason: Searched Parts I to III before ch10: 'port' means a switch port or a NAT table entry, never the transport-layer number that names a program. Fig 10.1 and ch10-attacks-p4 depend on it, and it is the one thing UDP adds to IP.
judge_fix: In ch10-udp-p1: 'an eight-byte header on top of IP: two port numbers that name the program at each end (53 is the DNS server's), a length and a checksum.'

quote: The paper's fix centred on two pieces, explained next: slow start and AIMD
problem: AIMD is named here, as a key-term chip, and then never expanded or named in the prose. p6 describes halving and linear growth without saying that this is AIMD. The expansion appears only in Fig 10.5's closed strip and in the math callout p8, which then expands it a second time.
fix: In p6, after 'in a sawtooth pattern': 'Adding a constant and halving is AIMD: additive increase, multiplicative decrease.' Then drop the parenthetical expansion at the start of p8.
reason: AIMD is chipped in p5, and p6 describes halving and linear growth without ever naming it. The first expansion sits in the closed Fig 10.5 strip, and the math callout expands it again.
judge_fix: In p6, after 'in a sawtooth pattern': 'Adding a constant on the way up and halving on the way down is AIMD: additive increase, multiplicative decrease.' Then in p8 drop the parenthetical, so it opens 'AIMD is the only one...' (see #16).

quote: begins cautiously, with a tiny congestion window (cwnd) of one segment
problem: The congestion window gets a name and nothing more. The prose never says it is a second limit the sender sets for itself and obeys alongside the receiver's window. That step exists only in Fig 10.4's closed strip ('The sender obeys the smaller'). A reader who knows only the receive window cannot tell whose window is being halved.
fix: 'Slow start begins cautiously, with a congestion window (cwnd), a second limit the sender sets for itself and obeys alongside the receiver's window, of one segment, and doubles it on every successful round trip.'
reason: p4 says only that something other than the receive window is needed. p6 then introduces cwnd with no word on how it relates to the receive window. That relation is stated only in the closed Fig 10.4 strip.
judge_fix: 'Slow start begins cautiously. The sender keeps a second limit of its own, the congestion window (cwnd), and obeys the smaller of it and the receiver's window; cwnd starts at one segment and _doubles_ on every successful round trip: exponential growth probes the network's capacity quickly.'

quote: In every ACK, the receiver advertises how much of its receive buffer remains free: the receive window.
problem: Section 02 (ch10-why-p2) already taught the window and 'in flight' ('Receivers periodically advertise a window ... senders never have more than that many in flight'). This paragraph teaches both from scratch again, and caption p3 defines 'in flight' a third time. The two passages also disagree: 'periodically' in why-p2, 'in every ACK' here and in caption p3.
fix: In ch10-why-p2, change 'Receivers periodically advertise' to 'Every acknowledgement also carries'. In ch10-aimd-p2, start from what the reader has: 'The first piece is the sliding window, built on the window from Section 02, which every ACK carries: the sender never has more than that many bytes in flight. As ACKs arrive, ...'
reason: The 'periodically' versus 'in every ACK' disagreement is real, and ch10-aimd-p2 re-teaches the window from scratch. Keep the 'in flight' gloss, because why-p2 never defines it and its key-term chip currently sits in the Fig 10.4 caption.
judge_fix: ch10-why-p2: 'Every acknowledgement also advertises a *window* (how many more bytes the receiver has buffer space to accept), and senders never have more than that many in flight.' ch10-aimd-p2 opening: 'The first piece is the *sliding window*, built on that receive window: the sender never has more than that many bytes in flight (sent but not yet acknowledged).' Keep the rest of p2, and drop the in-flight chip from the caption.

quote: The receiver sets the window size in every ACK, so a slow reader throttles a fast writer
problem: The caption teaches p2 again: 'in flight' defined again, the window set in every ACK, and flow control restated as 'a slow reader throttles a fast writer'. It should name the picture instead.
fix: 'Bytes 100 to 114 with a six-byte window: each ACK moves the left edge up to the byte it names, and as many cells open on the right.'
reason: The caption redefines 'in flight', restates that the window is set in every ACK, and adds the slogan about a slow reader throttling a fast writer, all of which p2 just said. It should name the picture.
judge_fix: 'Bytes 100 to 114 with a six-byte window: each ACK moves the left edge up to the byte it names, and as many cells open on the right.' (The in-flight chip moves to p2, see #7.)

quote: Slow start doubles the window every round trip until the first loss; after that TCP adds one segment
problem: The caption's first sentence repeats p6 almost word for word.
fix: 'One connection on a path that carries 24 segments: slow start overshoots to 32, then the window saws between about 12 and 25. TCP never measures the capacity; it finds the limit by overshooting it.'
reason: The caption's first sentence repeats p6 almost verbatim. The figure's own numbers (24, 32, 12 to 25) are what the caption should carry.
judge_fix: 'One connection on a path that carries 24 segments: slow start overshoots to 32, then the window saws between about 12 and 25. TCP never measures the capacity; it finds the limit by overshooting it.' Then cut the strip item 'This run', which would now repeat the caption.

quote: When it ends, both sides know each other's starting sequence numbers
problem: 'it' comes right after 'A TCP connection begins...', so it reads as the connection ending. The sentence means the handshake ending. A reader has to go back to sort this out.
fix: 'When the third arrives, both sides know each other's starting sequence numbers, ...'
reason: 'When it ends' directly follows 'A TCP connection begins...', so 'it' reads as the connection ending.
judge_fix: 'When the exchange is complete, both sides know each other's starting sequence numbers, both have allocated a TCB, and both are ready to stream.'

quote: a returning client can send its request in its very first packet
problem: The caption repeats p6 word for word. Its second sentence ('QUIC carries TLS 1.3 inside it and runs over UDP, in the application rather than the kernel') repeats both p6 and the strip's 'The stacks' item, so the same point is made three times.
fix: Caption: 'Over TCP and TLS 1.3 the page arrives after three round trips; QUIC's combined handshake makes it two, and a resumed connection one.' In the strip, cut the first sentence of 'The stacks' and keep the iterability point.
reason: The caption repeats p6's 'a returning client can send its request in its very first packet' word for word. Its second sentence repeats p6 again, and the strip's first 'The stacks' sentence says the same a third time.
judge_fix: Caption: 'Over TCP and TLS 1.3 the page arrives after three round trips; QUIC's combined handshake makes it two, and a resumed connection one.' Strip 'The stacks': 'QUIC ships with the browser or server, not the operating system, so it can change as fast as they do: its *iterability*.'

quote: No connection, no order, no retransmission: a lost datagram is simply missing
problem: The caption restates p1 (eight-byte header; no connection, no order, no retransmission). The strip restates p1 ('RFC 768 ... three pages long') and p2 (DNS fits in one datagram; voice and games would rather lose than wait). The figure's text adds nothing the prose has not just said.
fix: Caption: 'Port 51234 asks port 53 a DNS question with eight bytes of header. Datagram 2 is lost and nothing notices; retrying, if anyone does, is the application's job.' Strip: cut 'is three pages long' and the 'Where it wins' item.
reason: The caption restates p1 (eight bytes, no connection, no order, no retransmission). The strip's 'three pages long' repeats p1, and 'Where it wins' restates p2.
judge_fix: Caption: 'Port 51234 asks port 53 a DNS question with eight bytes of header. Datagram 2 is lost and nothing notices; retrying, if anyone does, is the application's job.' Strip: keep 'The standard' as 'RFC 768 is from August 1980. The checksum is optional over IPv4 and required over IPv6.' and cut 'Where it wins'.

quote: UDP's strength is that it has no state. TCP's strength is that it has all the state that reliability requires.
problem: An aphorism closer built on a parallel pair. It repeats Section 01 ('no state' in Fig 10.1's title), and Section 06 opens with the same antithesis ('TCP's strength is ... TCP's weakness is the same'), so two sections share one shape.
fix: Cut both sentences. The paragraph ends on the million TCBs, and Section 06 picks up the cost.
reason: The antithesis pair summarises the paragraph. The UDP half has no prose antecedent, because Section 01 says 'no state' only in the figure title. Section 06 reuses the same shape, so the pair reads as a template. The paragraph ends better on the million TCBs.
judge_fix: Cut the last two sentences ('UDP's strength is that it has no state. TCP's strength is...'), ending the paragraph on 'A Linux server with a million open TCP connections holds a million TCBs in kernel memory.'

quote: is not merely a combination that works; it is the only one that does
problem: The callout opens with a 'Not X; Y' reveal and closes on an aphorism ('forced by the mathematics, not chosen by taste') that restates the proof's claim.
fix: Open with: 'Chiu and Jain proved in 1989 that AIMD is the only one of the four combinations of additive or multiplicative increase and decrease that converges to both efficiency ... and fairness ...'. Cut the last sentence.
reason: It has the 'not merely X; it is the only one' reveal and a kicker that repeats the proof's claim. The facts are right: Chiu and Jain 1989, and MIMD and AIAD fail to converge to fairness while MIAD diverges.
judge_fix: Open: 'Chiu and Jain proved in 1989 that AIMD is the only one of the four combinations of additive or multiplicative increase with additive or multiplicative decrease that converges to both *efficiency* (the network is fully utilised) _and_ *fairness* (every flow gets an equal share).' Keep the MIMD/AIAD/MIAD sentence. Cut the last sentence.

quote: the network can never authenticate who you are, only what you say
problem: An aphorism closer that is also wrong as written. The network does not authenticate what you say either. It delivers whatever a packet claims, source address included, which is the point of the Mitnick story.
fix: 'The deeper lesson is that a packet's source address is only a claim, which the network carries but never checks, so applications must authenticate cryptographically on top.'
reason: The sentence is an aphorism closer, and it is imprecise: the network authenticates neither the sender nor the content. The Mitnick story shows that a source address is only a claim.
judge_fix: 'The deeper lesson is that a packet's source address is only a claim, which the network carries but never checks, so applications must authenticate cryptographically on top.'

quote: The defences are nearly all about making the protocol stateless under attack
problem: Two of the three examples it gives keep state (random ISNs, TLS). The strip's own last sentence says patches 'push state into harder places', which contradicts 'stateless'. 'state in the unguessable' does not name anything concrete.
fix: 'The defences mostly move state where an attacker cannot reach or forge it: SYN cookies (state in the wire), random ISNs (state an outsider cannot guess), TLS (state cryptographically authenticated).'
reason: Random ISNs and TLS do not make anything stateless, and the strip's own last sentence says patches 'push state into harder places'. 'state in the unguessable' names nothing concrete.
judge_fix: 'The defences mostly move state where an attacker cannot reach or forge it: SYN cookies (state in the wire), random ISNs (state an outsider cannot guess), TLS (state cryptographically authenticated).'

quote: TCP hijacking
problem: The glossary key-term chip wraps 'TCP' alone inside the bold 'TCP hijacking'. It renders as a cyan mono chip followed by bold 'hijacking', in the last section of the TCP chapter, and makes the glossary send TCP to Section 06. 'three-way handshake' is chipped in ch10-attacks-p2, so its glossary entry also lands in Section 06, not Section 03 (glossary.json: tcp → ch10-attacks, three-way handshake → ch10-attacks).
fix: Make 'TCP hijacking' plain bold. Move the TCP chip to 'TCP' in ch10-why-p1 and the three-way-handshake chip to ch10-handshake-p1. Then run npm run build:glossary.
reason: The wrapper is `TCP hijacking`, which renders as a chip followed by bold text. The glossary then sends TCP and three-way handshake to Section 06, although both are taught earlier. UNDER.md lists the TCP chip as a declined 'extractor quirk', but it is a visible glitch and a misdirected glossary link. Note that 'three-way handshake' does not appear in handshake-p1, so the wording must be added.
judge_fix: Make 'TCP hijacking' plain bold. Chip TCP in ch10-why-p1 (`TCP`). In ch10-handshake-p1 start 'A TCP connection begins with the three-way handshake: three messages (TCP calls each one a segment)...', and remove the chip from ch10-attacks-p2 (leave the phrase bold). Then run npm run build:glossary and check for garbled entries.

quote: The trick: the source IP could be forged
problem: The emphasis covers 'the source IP could' instead of the one contrasted word, so the stress lands wrongly. 'The trick:' is also a clipped opener.
fix: 'But the source IP could be forged, if you also knew TCP's sequence numbers.'
reason: The em wraps 'the source IP could' instead of the contrast word 'could'. The glossary tooltip pass also treats em spans as candidates.
judge_fix: 'But the source IP could be forged, if you also knew TCP's sequence numbers.'

quote: ISN generator was barely random at all
problem: A mixed idiom. The same sentence says each ISN stepped up by a fixed 128,000, which means not random at all.
fix: 'And Shimomura's machines' ISN generator was not random at all: minutes of probing ... showed each new connection's ISN stepping up by a fixed 128,000, ...'
reason: 'Barely random at all' contradicts the same sentence's fixed 128,000 stride, which is not random at all. The possessive stack is also clumsy.
judge_fix: 'And the ISN generator on Shimomura's machines was not random at all: minutes of probing on Christmas afternoon showed each new connection's ISN stepping up by a fixed 128,000, so the next one was predictable.'

quote: It is what the great majority of internet TCP traffic runs.
problem: Traffic does not 'run' an algorithm, and the sentence reads as if a word is missing.
fix: 'Most of the internet's TCP traffic uses it.'
reason: The grammar is loose, and the claim is also wrong. The Mishra et al. census (SIGMETRICS 2020) found CUBIC on about 36 percent of the top 20,000 sites but BBR carrying an estimated 40 percent or more of traffic by volume. 'The great majority of internet TCP traffic' also sits badly beside p4's BBR-at-Google claim.
judge_fix: 'It is the most widely deployed variant, though BBR carries a large share of the traffic by volume.' Source: Mishra, Sun, Jain, Ng, Leong, 'The Great Internet TCP Congestion Control Census', SIGMETRICS 2020.

quote: where round-trip times were tens of milliseconds and bandwidths a few megabits
problem: Section 04 has just told the reader that the 1986 LBL–Berkeley link was designed for 32 kilobits per second. 'a few megabits' for the same era is a hundred times more, and nothing reconciles the two.
fix: 'where round-trip times were tens of milliseconds and links ran at kilobits to a few megabits per second.'
reason: Section 04 has just given a 32 kbit/s link for 1986. NSFNET ran at 56 kbit/s in 1986 and at T1 only from 1988, so 'a few megabits' for the late 1980s overshoots the book's own example.
judge_fix: 'where round-trip times were tens to hundreds of milliseconds and links ran at tens of kilobits to a few megabits per second.'

quote: Its protocol, which they called simply TCP
problem: TCP is never expanded anywhere in the book (the glossary says Transmission Control Protocol), while TCB is expanded two paragraphs later. 'simply' implies there is nothing to expand. In 1974 the letters stood for Transmission Control Program.
fix: 'Its protocol, the Transmission Control Program (TCP; the P later became Protocol), was designed to do four things...'
reason: TCP is never expanded in the book's prose (only in the glossary), while TCB is. Cerf and Kahn's 1974 paper called the module a Transmission Control Program, so 'simply TCP' hides the expansion at the natural spot.
judge_fix: 'Its design, the Transmission Control Program (TCP; the last word later became Protocol), was meant to do four things on top of an unreliable packet network: ...'

quote: Four would be redundant.
problem: A clipped closer that asserts without saying why. The reason is that the server's acknowledgement and its own SYN ride in one segment.
fix: 'A fourth is not needed because the server's acknowledgement and its own starting number travel together in the SYN-ACK.'
reason: The paragraph's job is to give reasons for the count, and 'Four would be redundant.' asserts without one. The real reason is a single clause.
judge_fix: 'A fourth is not needed, because the server's acknowledgement and its own starting number travel together in the SYN-ACK.'

quote: each move triggered by an arriving segment, a program call or a timer
problem: This repeats p3 ('A segment arriving, a call from the program or a timer running out moves it').
fix: 'TCP's eleven states, as RFC 793 defined them in 1981: the client connects and closes first, the server listens and closes second. The side that closes first waits in TIME_WAIT ...'
reason: The caption's trigger clause repeats p3 ('A segment arriving, a call from the program or a timer running out moves it...').
judge_fix: Caption: 'TCP's eleven states, as RFC 793 defined them in 1981: the client connects and closes first, the server listens and closes second. The side that closes first waits in TIME_WAIT so that stray packets from this connection die before its addresses and ports are reused.'

quote: The last two decades produced three answers.
problem: It announces what the section title has just said ('Three answers to TCP's mid-life crisis').
fix: Cut the sentence. p2 opens on CUBIC directly.
reason: It announces what the section title ('Three answers...') has just said, and p2 opens on CUBIC directly. This is law 2's 'announcing' case.
judge_fix: Cut 'The last two decades produced three answers.'

quote: a keyed hash of the (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port, time bucket)
problem: Hashes are first taught in Ch11 §04 (ch11-crypto); nothing earlier in the book mentions them. The SYN cookie mechanism relies on what a keyed hash guarantees.
fix: 'a keyed hash (a scrambled 32-bit fingerprint that only the holder of the secret key can compute) of the source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port and a time bucket, ...'
reason: Hashing is first taught in Ch11 section 04. The SYN-cookie idea needs the reader to know a keyed hash is an unforgeable fingerprint of the connection's identifiers.
judge_fix: 'a keyed hash (a scrambled fingerprint) of the source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port and a time bucket, small enough to fit in 32 bits and hard to forge without the server's secret key.'

quote: the W_max both flows had reached when the loss came

fix: Write W<sub>max</sub> in the strip and its formula: W(t) = C(t − K)³ + W<sub>max</sub>, K = ∛(W<sub>max</sub> × 0.3 / C).

quote: the client connects and closes first, the server listens and closes second
problem: The animation plays the server's whole life first (listen, SYN in, ACK in, FIN in, close(): send FIN, ACK in, about 2 to 8.5 s), then the client's (connect, SYN-ACK in, close(): send FIN, ..., about 10.4 to 15.6 s). So 'server: FIN in: send ACK' and 'server: close(): send FIN' light up before the client has even connected, let alone sent its FIN. That puts cause after effect and contradicts the caption's 'client ... closes first, the server ... closes second'.
fix: Interleave the twelve steps in causal order, keeping both rings visible and the same 16 s loop: server: listen() → client: connect(): send SYN → server: SYN in: send SYN-ACK → client: SYN-ACK in: send ACK → server: ACK in → client: close(): send FIN → server: FIN in: send ACK → client: ACK in → server: close(): send FIN → client: FIN in: send ACK → server: ACK in → client: wait 2 × max segment lifetime.
reason: Checked the SVG keyTimes in fig-10-3 (public/part-3.html, 16 s loop). Server steps light at 0.134 to 0.527 (2.1 to 8.4 s), client steps only at 0.647 to 0.975 (10.4 to 15.6 s). So 'server: FIN in: send ACK' (5.3 s) and 'server: close(): send FIN' (6.4 s) light before the client has connected. That is effect before cause. It also contradicts the caption's 'the client connects and closes first, the server listens and closes second'. A reader watching the two sides will see it.
judge_fix: Retime the twelve steps in causal order, same 16 s loop, same equal slots (about 0.0656 of the loop, 1.05 s each, starting at the current 0.134). Order: server: listen() > client: connect(): send SYN > server: SYN in: send SYN-ACK > client: SYN-ACK in: send ACK > server: ACK in > client: close(): send FIN > server: FIN in: send ACK > client: ACK in > server: close(): send FIN > client: FIN in: send ACK > server: ACK in > client: wait 2 × max segment lifetime. Each edge highlight and its y=460 label take the same slot. Each walking token keeps its opacity window from its first to its last step and holds its position while the other side moves. Change only the animation timing. The caption text stays as it is, since it already says client first, server second.

quote: a returning client can send its request in its very first packet
problem: This clause appears word for word in ch10-modern-p6, the paragraph right above the figure. The caption's second sentence ('QUIC carries TLS 1.3 inside it and runs over UDP, in the application rather than the kernel') restates p6's 'runs over UDP ... inside the application, not the kernel'. The reader gets the same words twice in a row (law 2).
fix: Make the caption read the picture: "Over TCP a browser spends one round trip on TCP's handshake and another on TLS's before it can ask for the page: three in all. QUIC carries TLS 1.3 inside it, so one handshake does both jobs (two), and a resumed connection gets the page after one."
reason: Checked the packet. The caption's clause 'a returning client can send its request in its very first packet' is word for word in ch10-modern-p6, the paragraph directly above. The caption's second sentence also restates p6's 'runs over UDP ... inside the application, not the kernel'. That is law 2 repetition, back to back. The finding's proposed wording has a counting slip: 'before it can ask for the page: three in all' reads as three before asking, but the picture counts TCP handshake, TLS and the GET, so the page arrives after three.
judge_fix: Replace the caption with: "Over TCP a browser spends one round trip on TCP's handshake and another on TLS's, then a third to fetch the page. QUIC carries TLS 1.3 inside it, so one handshake does both jobs and the page arrives after two; a returning client gets it after one." Leave p6 as it is. The caption has no key-term spans, so the glossary is unaffected.

quote: TCP's eleven states, as RFC 793 defined them in 1981
problem: The picture draws twelve boxes, because CLOSED appears twice (top and bottom) and nothing says the two are the same state. A reader who counts the boxes against the caption's 'eleven' gets twelve.
fix: Label the bottom box "CLOSED (again)", or add to the key line: "CLOSED is drawn twice: where a connection starts and where it ends".
reason: Counted the boxes in fig-10-3: CLOSED, SYN_SENT, LISTEN, SYN_RCVD, ESTABLISHED, FIN_WAIT_1, CLOSE_WAIT, FIN_WAIT_2, CLOSING, LAST_ACK, TIME_WAIT, CLOSED. That is twelve boxes. The caption and desc say 'eleven', which is correct for RFC 793 (11 distinct states). Nothing says CLOSED is drawn twice. A reader who counts will stop. The fix is cheap. The legend lines at the bottom are already full width, so the note goes in the caption.
judge_fix: In ch10-handshake-p4 change the opening to: "TCP's eleven states (CLOSED is drawn twice, where a connection starts and where it ends), as RFC 793 defined them in 1981: the client connects and closes first, ...". The rest of the caption stays. Optionally add the same parenthesis to the desc.

quote: ACK 109: it slides on
problem: At 5.8 to 6.1 s the window frame glides backwards from 109–114 to 100–105 while the label still reads 'ACK 109: it slides on' and every cell is still acked. A TCP window never moves back. At 2.2 to 2.5 s and 9.0 to 9.3 s the frame starts sliding forward before the ACK label and the cell colours change, so for 0.3 s orange in-flight bytes sit outside the window while the label says 'sent 106 to 108: full again' or 'window full: wait for an ACK'.
fix: Make the loop reset a cut: hold translate 216 until 0.6095, then jump to 0. Start each forward slide only after the ACK label and the cell colours have switched, moving the slides from 0.22–0.25 to 0.25–0.28 and from 0.90–0.93 to 0.93–0.96, or switch the label and cells at 0.22 and 0.90.
reason: Checked the window frame's animateTransform in fig-10-4 (10 s loop): keyTimes 0;.06;.09;.22;.25;.58;.60995;.61;.74;.77;.90;.93;1 with values 72;72;72;72;216;216;0;0;0;0;0;72;72. The frame glides back from 216 to 0 between 0.58 and 0.61 (5.8 to 6.1 s) while the label still reads 'ACK 109: it slides on' and all cells are acked. A TCP window never moves back. The forward slides at .22 to .25 and .90 to .93 begin about 0.3 s before the label and cell colours switch at .2495 and .929, so the window moves ahead of the ACK. Real but small.
judge_fix: Edit only the window's translate animation. Replace its keyTimes with "0;0.25;0.28;0.60995;0.61;0.93;0.96;1" and its values with "72 0;72 0;216 0;216 0;0 0;0 0;72 0;72 0". The loop reset becomes a cut at 0.61, where the cells already flip, and each forward slide starts after its ACK label and cell colours have changed. Cells and labels keep their keyTimes.

quote: each ACK names the next byte expected, the window's left edge moves up to it, and room opens on the right
problem: The caption retells ch10-aimd-p2 in other words: in flight means sent but not acknowledged, the trailing edge advances, room opens at the leading edge, the receiver sets the window in every ACK, flow control. It never points at what the picture shows.
fix: Tie it to the drawn values: "ACK 103 says bytes 100 to 102 arrived, so the six-byte window moves up to 103 and three new bytes may go; ACK 109 moves it on by six. The receiver restates that six in every ACK, so a slow reader throttles a fast writer with no extra messages."
reason: Checked ch10-aimd-p2 against the caption. Both say the sender keeps at most a window's worth in flight (sent but not acknowledged), the trailing edge or left edge advances, new bytes go at the leading edge or room opens on the right, the receiver advertises the window in every ACK, and this is flow control. The caption never refers to the drawn values (ACK 103, ACK 109, six bytes), so it restates the paragraph above it (law 2). Caution: 'in flight' is a key-term span in this caption and the glossary entry 'in flight' is anchored to section ch10-aimd. Keep the span, then run npm run build:glossary.
judge_fix: Replace the caption with: "ACK 103 says bytes 100 to 102 arrived, so the six-byte window moves up to 103 and three more bytes may go; ACK 109 moves it on by six. The sender keeps at most a window's worth of bytes in flight, and because the receiver restates the window in every ACK, a slow reader throttles a fast writer with no extra messages." Both sentences match the picture: window 100 to 105, then 103 to 108, then 109 to 114.

quote: SYN · let's connect, I count from X
problem: The travelling dots follow two colour rules at once. The SYN-ACK dot is the server's red and the ACK dot is the client's green, but the SYN dot, also sent by the client, is the arrow blue. A reader who notices the colours cannot tell what they mean.
fix: Colour the SYN dot the client's green (rgba(150,216,150,0.95)) to match the ACK dot, or make all three dots the arrow blue.
reason: Checked the hero SVG in part-3.html. The SYN dot (circle cy=160) is rgba(79,196,230,0.95), the arrow blue. The SYN-ACK dot (cy=240) is the server's red rgba(232,120,120,0.95), and the ACK dot (cy=320) is the client's green rgba(150,216,150,0.95). The client box is green and the server box red. Two of the three dots follow the sender-colour rule and the first, also from the client, breaks it. Small but real, and a one-value fix.
judge_fix: Change the SYN dot's fill from rgba(79,196,230,0.95) to rgba(150,216,150,0.95), the client's green, so all three dots take the colour of their sender.
